body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: The Doldrum, or 1819, which has been revived at this Theatre, is the last convulsive laugh of Mr. O'Keefe's expiring Muse; and a doldrum is, we believe, the cant word for a long sleeper.

The farce completely usurps the province of pantomime. The first act is made out by the self-elevation of two valets into the situations of their masters; they meet at a tavern, mutually impose upon each other, and are exposed, like the butler who invited the Vicar of Wakefield to his master's house, by the unexpected arrival of the real owner of the mansion. Two old gentlemen then come into play. Sir Marmaduke (Mr. Munden) and Septimus (Mr. Mathews). The former is a gross caricature, who walks about loose with Trussler's Chronology in his pocket, diverting his attention from the most serious concerns of his life, by searching for such petty, peddling information, as seems to him to grow out of the words which are employed in conversation with him: thus, when his oldest friend escapes from a French prison and arrives to England in a ship, he interrupts the narrative to tell when ships were first invented, that the idea of them was derived from the Nautilus, &c. The latter, we believe, is meant merely for a credulous old fool; and a precious and most voracious believer he is; for he can be persuaded that the repose of a single night has been a diseased sleep of seven whole years; and that during that time he has been created a peer, by the title of Baron Septimus, for the services which his long sleep has conferred upon his country,—that the fashion of dress has in the interim changed to drab-coloured coats and large blue and white wigs, which are worn alike by men and women,—that a canary-bird he brought with him from abroad is grown to a large golden hen,—and that stair-cases and stairs are obsolete, spring-chairs for the gentry, and pulleyed baskets for menials, having superseded them;—and, to crown the pantomime, a peck loaf is brought in as the penny roll of the year 1819, and a rib of beef as the mutton chop. The plot is this: the two old gentlemen being both blindly contradictious, a union cannot be effected between the son and daughter of each, till the latter shall be of age at 25 years, seven years from the time of the representation, supposed to be at 1812. Neither father has the least real objection to the match; but as one party must propose that it shall take place immediately, that is reason sufficient for the other to say it shall not; and so they go on changing the shall and shall not from month to month, till the negative ends with Septimus; and yet these two drivellers are represented as having been fellow-wranglers at College! A scheme is then set on foot to persuade Septimus that he has in one night slept the seven years, during which the couple were to perform quarantine; and the whole family disguise themselves in various masquerade characters to keep up the deception, which the sleeper detects only by feigning, that, if the year 1819 be arrived, it had long ago been foretold to him, that at the very hour which the clock then strikes, he should die: he accordingly begins to work upon the feelings of his son, who, alarmed lest the old gentleman's imagination should persuade him his hour was come seven years before it had arrived, confesses the trick; and there an end. Forgiveness and immediate union follow, as naturally as absolution after confession. There was some scope for humour and satire in the anticipation of the customs, changes, and refinements, which the lapse of seven years might produce—and the French reader will naturally think of the Memoirs de l'an 2440; but Mr. O'Keefe has laboriously avoided almost every opportunity of being witty, and after the prophetic penny roll and mutton chop, we are sure we shall be spared all further inquiry. What would not Swift have made of such an idea!

The farce is inimitably performed on the parts of Messrs. Munden and Mathews. The delightful peerings about the coat of a gentleman, in order to reconnoitre the number of buttons on it, before he entraps him into a wager as to their amount, are the very quintessence of grimace; and his sly manner of informing the audience that there are "Four upon the cuffs," has been surpassed by nothing, but his "Some gentleman has left his liquor," in the Turnpike Gate. Sir Marmaduke's comment upon that man's ignorance, who does not know how many buttons he has upon his coat, was one of the few good touches in the Doldrum. Mr. Mathew's old man is a worthy companion to that of Mr. Munden, never so overpoweringly droll, but looked and spoken with more of the smack of age than Mr. Munden can assume.—The test of the farce is only competently played; and there were many auditors on Wednesday night, who summed up all our objections to the drama in one pregnant and more potent hiss, when the curtain dropped.
